answer:
IA QUALIFICATIONS AND AUTHORITY REGARDING MAJOR ALTERATIONS — 14 CFR REFERENCE PACKAGE (FAA-AMT CONTEXT)

=====================================================================
0. DIRECT ANSWER
=====================================================================
The question splits into two questions that are answered by two different sections. Both must be stated, because 'qualifications' means one thing and 'regarding major alterations' means another.

(A) WHO MAY HOLD AN IA (eligibility) — 14 CFR 65.91.
    An applicant must be a certificated A&P mechanic, must have held both ratings for at least 3 years, must have been actively engaged in maintaining certificated aircraft for at least 2 of the 3 years before applying, must have a fixed base of operations, must be English-proficient, and must pass the FAA's inspection authorization written test.

(B) WHAT AN IA MUST SATISFY TO APPROVE A MAJOR ALTERATION (authority + conditions) — 14 CFR 65.95(a)(1).
    There is NO separate 'major alteration qualification' beyond holding a current IA. The qualifier is a DATA condition, not an extra certificate. An IA may inspect and approve for return to service an aircraft, part, or appliance after a major repair or major alteration ONLY IF all three of the following are true:
      (B1) the aircraft is NOT maintained under a continuous airworthiness program under Part 121; and
      (B2) the work was done in accordance with technical data APPROVED BY THE ADMINISTRATOR; and
      (B3) the work was done in accordance with Part 43.

VERBATIM TEXT — 14 CFR 65.95(a)(1) (eCFR, fetched 2026-11-15T21:17:18Z, sha256 04eedc455339):
"(a) The holder of an inspection authorization may—
 (1) Inspect and approve for return to service any aircraft or related part or appliance (except any aircraft maintained in accordance with a continuous airworthiness program under part 121 of this chapter) after a major repair or major alteration to it in accordance with part 43 [New] of this chapter, if the work was done in accordance with technical data approved by the Administrator; and"

FAA IA Information Guide confirms the same basic-function statement:
"The basic functions of the holder of an inspection authorization (IA) are set forth in Title 14 of the Code of Federal Regulations (14 CFR) part 65, § 65.95. With the exception of aircraft maintained in accordance with a Continuous Airworthiness Maintenance Program under part 121, an IA may inspect and approve for return to service any aircraft or related part or appliance after a major repair or major alteration." (faa.gov ia_info_guide.pdf, fetched 2026-11-15T21:17:23Z, sha256 ece24efe31ea)

=====================================================================
1. REGULATORY MAP — WHICH SECTION ANSWERS WHICH QUESTION
=====================================================================
| # | Question | Citation | What it supplies |
|---|----------|----------|------------------|
| 1 | Who may be issued an IA | 14 CFR 65.91 | Eligibility criteria (A&P 3 yr, 2-of-3 yr activity, fixed base, English, test) |
| 2 | How long the IA lasts | 14 CFR 65.92 | Two-year cycle; expires 31 March of the first odd-numbered year after issuance |
| 3 | How the IA is kept alive | 14 CFR 65.93 | Renewal by activity or recurrent training during the preceding 24 months |
| 4 | What the IA may do with a major alteration | 14 CFR 65.95(a)(1) | Inspect and approve for return to service, subject to B1/B2/B3 above |
| 5 | What an alteration IS (major vs minor) | 14 CFR 1.1 definition; Part 43 Appendix A | Major alteration = one that might appreciably affect weight, balance, structural strength, performance, powerplant operation, flight characteristics, or other airworthiness qualities; Appendix A enumerates |
| 6 | Who may approve work for return to service | 14 CFR 43.7 | Appropriately rated person / IA / repair station |
| 7 | What the record entry must contain | 14 CFR 43.9 | Description, date, signer, certificate number, approval basis |
| 8 | Major alteration record form and distribution | Part 43 Appendix B | FAA Form 337, at least in duplicate; copy to owner; copy to FAA Aircraft Registration Branch (Oklahoma City) within 48 hours after approval for RTS |
| 9 | Operator recordkeeping | 14 CFR 91.417 (Part 91) | Retention of maintenance records, including Form 337 |
| 10 | Data approval vs data acceptance | AC 43-210A; FAA Order 8300.16; field approval process | Approved data sources; when a field approval (Form 337 Block 3) is required |

=====================================================================
2. (A) ELIGIBILITY CHECKLIST — 14 CFR 65.91
=====================================================================
Apply in order; every line must be YES before an application is valid.

[ ] E-1  Holds a currently effective mechanic certificate with BOTH an Airframe rating and a Powerplant rating.
[ ] E-2  Both ratings have been in effect for a total of at least 3 years.
[ ] E-3  Has been actively engaged, for at least 2 of the 3 years before the application date, in maintaining aircraft certificated and maintained under 14 CFR.
[ ] E-4  Has a fixed base of operations at which he/she can be located in person or by telephone during a normal working week (this need not be the place where the authority is exercised).
[ ] E-5  Can read, write, speak, and understand the English language.
[ ] E-6  Has passed the FAA inspection authorization written test.
[ ] E-7  Application filed with the FAA on the mechanic's application form (FAA Form 8610-1).

Currency after issuance (needed before ANY 65.95 signature):
[ ] E-8  Authorization not expired. Per 65.92 the IA runs on a two-year cycle expiring 31 March of the first odd-numbered year after issuance; renewal per 65.93 is activity-based or training-based over the preceding 24 months.

SOURCE-STATUS FLAG: lines E-1 through E-7 are stated from the regulation as generally known and were NOT verified against a fetched eCFR passage during this session (the verified set contains only 65.95(a)(1), Part 43, Form 337 material). Before this package is used for a training or compliance document, open https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-14/chapter-I/subchapter-D/part-65/subpart-D/section-65.91 and confirm each line. Do NOT rely on any recollection of the specific 65.93 renewal counts/hours from this package — that section is deliberately not quantified here.

=====================================================================
3. (B) ELEMENT-BY-ELEMENT COMPLIANCE TEST — 14 CFR 65.95(a)(1)
=====================================================================
Each element is a gate. Failure of any single gate means the IA may not sign the approval for return to service.

ELEMENT 1 — CURRENT AUTHORIZATION
  Test: Is the IA currently effective (not expired, renewed per 65.93)?
  Evidence: certificate + IA date; renewal record.
  Fail action: decline; no signature.

ELEMENT 2 — ITEM IS AN AIRCRAFT, PART, OR APPLIANCE
  Test: Is the subject within 'any aircraft or related part or appliance'?
  Note: this excludes items that are not aircraft/articles (e.g., ground support equipment) and excludes work outside the airworthiness framework.

ELEMENT 3 — NOT A PART 121 CONTINUOUS AIRWORTHINESS PROGRAM AIRCRAFT  ← express statutory exclusion, not a policy preference
  Test: Is the aircraft maintained under a continuous airworthiness program under Part 121?
  If YES: the IA has NO 65.95(a)(1) approval authority for that major repair/alteration. Route to the operator's Part 121 approved program.
  Evidence: operator identity, OpSpecs/Part 121 status.

ELEMENT 4 — WORK FOLLOWED TECHNICAL DATA APPROVED BY THE ADMINISTRATOR  ← the element most often failed
  Test: Does an APPROVED data source exist that covers this specific alteration on this specific aircraft/model?
  Typical APPROVED data: Type Certificate / ATC data and TCDS; Supplemental Type Certificate (STC) and its drawings/ICA; Airworthiness Directives; Parts Manufacturer Approval data installed per its approval; DER-approved data (Form 8110-3); FAA field-approved data (Form 337 Block 3 signed by the FAA); AC 43.13-1B/2B data where the Administrator has approved it as the basis for that major repair/alteration.
  Typical ACCEPTABLE but NOT approved data (insufficient alone): manufacturer service bulletins/letters, vendor instructions, generic engineering practice, non-FAA drawings, AC 43.13 general practice not approved for the specific alteration.
  If only acceptable data exists: a FIELD APPROVAL (Form 337, FAA signature in Block 3) or DER approval is required BEFORE the IA can approve for return to service. An IA signature does not create approved data.
  Evidence: copy of the STC/drawing/AD/8110-3/Block 3 field approval, revision-identified.

ELEMENT 5 — WORK DONE IN ACCORDANCE WITH PART 43
  Test: Were methods, techniques, and practices at least equal to Part 43 (43.13), and were performance/recording rules (43.5, 43.7, 43.9, Appendix B) followed?
  Evidence: work order, conformity inspection record, Form 337 draft, logbook entry.

ELEMENT 6 — PERSONAL INSPECTION BY THE IA
  Principle: the authority in 65.95 is conferred on 'the holder' personally. The IA cannot delegate the conformity inspection or sign off on work someone else inspected. FAA guidance (IA Information Guide) frames the IA's primary responsibility as determining airworthiness by inspecting repairs or alterations for conformity to approved data and assuring the aircraft is in a condition for safe operation. (Guidance, not CFR text — treat as FAA interpretation.)

ELEMENT 7 — AIRWORTHINESS DETERMINATION
  Test: After conformity, is the aircraft/part/appliance in a condition for safe operation and in compliance with applicable airworthiness requirements?
  If NO: do not approve. Record the discrepancy; do not sign Block 7.

=====================================================================
4. CONFORMITY INSPECTION PROTOCOL FOR A MAJOR ALTERATION
=====================================================================
Procedure P-1 through P-9. Holds (STOP conditions) are marked.

P-1  CLASSIFY. Determine major vs minor against 14 CFR 1.1 and Part 43 Appendix A. If major, Form 337 is required (Appendix B). HOLD if classification is contested — resolve before work proceeds.
P-2  IDENTIFY DATA. Obtain the approved data package (ELEMENT 4). HOLD if only acceptable data exists — route to field approval / DER.
P-3  VERIFY SCOPE. Confirm the data covers this model/serial and this configuration; check revision level.
P-4  PHYSICAL CONFORMITY INSPECTION. Verify, item by item:
       - materials, thickness, alloy/temper match the drawing
       - fastener type, diameter, grip length, count, spacing, edge distance
       - hole quality, deburring, interference-fit requirements
       - torque values applied and recorded where specified
       - corrosion protection, sealant, primer, drainage paths
       - structural load path continuity; no cut stringers/frames/spars without approved reinforcement
       - clearance to control cables, pulleys, bellcranks, fuel/ hydraulic/hydraulic lines, wiring
       - electrical load analysis and circuit protection for new equipment
       - bonding/grounding
       - finish and identification/placards
       - weight and balance impact computed and reflected in the equipment list / W&B record
       - flight manual supplement or AFM revision inserted where the data requires it
       - Instructions for Continued Airworthiness (ICA) incorporated into the operator's maintenance program
P-5  COMPATIBILITY CHECK. Confirm the alteration does not conflict with previously approved repairs/alterations (prior 337s, STCs, AD-mandated modifications). HOLD if there is interference — engineering reconciliation required.
P-6  AIRWORTHINESS DETERMINATION. Pass/fail per ELEMENT 7.
P-7  FORM 337. Ensure Block 6 (conformity statement by the person who performed the work) and Block 8 (description of work + references to approved data) are complete and accurate. Block 3 is FAA use only (field approval). The IA signs Block 7, Approval for Return to Service, with certificate number.
P-8  RECORDS. Make the maintenance record entry per 43.9 (description, date, signature, certificate number, approval basis). Provide the owner a signed copy of the Form 337. Forward a copy to the FAA Aircraft Registration Branch, Oklahoma City, within 48 hours after approval for return to service (Part 43 Appendix B).
P-9  OPERATOR RECORDS. Confirm the alteration is entered in the operator's records (91.417 for Part 91) and that the W&B/equipment list and AFM supplement are updated.

VERBATIM — Part 43 Appendix B (eCFR, sha256 61a4f2b93dcb):
"(1) Execute FAA Form 337 at least in duplicate; (2) Give a signed copy of that form to the aircraft owner; and (3) Forward a copy of that form to the FAA Aircraft Registration Branch in Oklahoma City, Oklahoma, within 48 hours after the aircraft, airframe, aircraft engine, propeller, or appliance is approved for return to service."

VERBATIM — Part 43 return-to-service rule (sha256 61a4f2b93dcb):
"To return an affected product to service, a person authorized in paragraph (c) of this section must approve (certify) maintenance, preventive maintenance, and alterations performed under this section..."

=====================================================================
5. TEST / VALIDATION CASES (deterministic pass-fail)
=====================================================================
TC-01  BASELINE CONFORMING. Part 91 Cessna 172; wingtip recognition light installed per STC; IA current; data = STC drawings + ICA; IA personally inspected; Blocks 6/7/8 complete; 337 forwarded within 48 h.
       EXPECTED: Approve for return to service. All records complete. PASS.
TC-02  PART 121 EXCLUSION. Major alteration presented on an aircraft maintained under a Part 121 continuous airworthiness program.
       EXPECTED: IA must DECLINE. 65.95(a)(1) express exclusion. Route to the operator's approved program. PASS if declined.
TC-03  ACCEPTABLE-ONLY DATA. Alteration supported only by a manufacturer service bulletin (not FAA-approved).
       EXPECTED: No IA approval. Require field approval (Form 337 Block 3) or DER-approved data first. PASS if refused.
TC-04  EXPIRED IA. Authorization lapsed 31 March of the odd-numbered year and not renewed.
       EXPECTED: Any Block 7 signature is invalid. FAIL if signed.
TC-05  NO PERSONAL INSPECTION. Owner performed the alteration; IA signs without inspecting.
       EXPECTED: Noncompliant. Authority is personal and non-delegable. FAIL if signed.
TC-06  WEIGHT AND BALANCE NOT UPDATED. Alteration changes empty weight/CG; equipment list and W&B not revised.
       EXPECTED: Withhold approval until W&B and any required flight manual supplement are updated. FAIL if approved as-is.
TC-07  ICA NOT INCORPORATED. STC carries Instructions for Continued Airworthiness; ICA not added to the maintenance program.
       EXPECTED: Withhold approval until ICA incorporated. FAIL if approved as-is.
TC-08  INCOMPATIBILITY. New antenna doubler conflicts with a prior skin repair on the same station.
       EXPECTED: HOLD; engineering reconciliation required before approval. FAIL if approved without reconciliation.
TC-09  48-HOUR FORWARDING MISSED. Form 337 executed but not sent to the FAA Aircraft Registration Branch within 48 hours.
       EXPECTED: Recordkeeping finding; correct the distribution. FAIL if uncorrected.
TC-10  MISCLASSIFICATION. An alteration listed as major under Part 43 Appendix A was handled as a logbook-only minor alteration.
       EXPECTED: Noncompliant; Form 337 required. FAIL if no 337.
TC-11  IA APPROVAL USED AS DATA APPROVAL. IA signs Block 7 where no approved data exists and Block 3 is unsigned.
       EXPECTED: Noncompliant. IA approval does not create approved data. FAIL if signed.
TC-12  OUT-OF-SCOPE CONTROL. Annual/progressive inspection privilege (65.95(a)(2)) invoked inside a major-alteration question.
       EXPECTED: Not applicable to the alteration approval; note and exclude. PASS (correctly excluded).

=====================================================================
6. AUDIT CHECKLIST — TOP FINDINGS AN IA REVIEW SHOULD CATCH
=====================================================================
1. Block 7 signed with no approved data behind Block 8.
2. Field approval assumed but Block 3 unsigned.
3. Part 121 CAMP aircraft approved under 65.95.
4. IA not current at date of signature.
5. Alteration approved without personal inspection.
6. Weight and balance / equipment list not updated.
7. Flight manual supplement not issued where required.
8. ICA not incorporated into the maintenance program.
9. Form 337 not forwarded within 48 hours, or not given to the owner.
10. Prior alteration compatibility not checked.
11. Minor/major misclassification against Part 43 Appendix A.
12. No revision identification on the approved data cited.

# Compliance answer — Qualifications for Inspection Authorization (IA) with respect to major alterations

Scope: U.S. FAA, 14 CFR as published on eCFR. Question as asked: 'what are the qualifications for inspection authorization regarding major alterations (FAA-AMT)'. Assumed (stated because the question does not say): the asker is a certificated aviation maintenance technician (A&P) or an AMT student asking about the Inspection Authorization under 14 CFR Part 65, Subpart D, and 'major alteration' is used in the 14 CFR 1.1 / Part 43 Appendix A sense.

## Bottom line

There is **no separate 'major alteration' rating or endorsement**. The qualification is the **Inspection Authorization (IA)** issued under **14 CFR Part 65, Subpart D**. Two questions must be kept apart, because they are answered by different sections:

| Question | Governing section |
|---|---|
| What qualifies a person to **hold** an IA? | **14 CFR 65.91** (application, eligibility), **65.92** (duration), **65.93** (renewal) |
| What may an IA **approve** after a major alteration? | **14 CFR 65.95(a)(1)**, with approval/record rules in **14 CFR 43.5, 43.7, 43.9(d)** |
| What counts as a 'major alteration'? | **14 CFR 1.1** (definition), **Part 43 Appendix A** (list) |

A mechanic certificate with airframe and powerplant ratings alone does **not** carry major-alteration approval authority for return to service; that approval requires an IA holder, a Part 145 repair station, or another person authorized under Part 43. Conversely, holding an IA does not create a free-standing right to approve any alteration — the alteration must have been accomplished using **technical data approved by the Administrator** (65.95(a)(1)).

## 1. Initial qualification for an Inspection Authorization — 14 CFR 65.91

| # | Requirement | Citation | Verification status |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Hold a **currently effective mechanic certificate with both an airframe rating and a powerplant rating**, each currently effective and **in effect for a total of at least 3 years** | 65.91(c)(1) | Cite-and-verify (read at eCFR link in §6) |
| 2 | Have been **actively engaged, for at least 2 of the 3 years before application**, in maintaining aircraft certificated and maintained under 14 CFR | 65.91(c)(2) | Cite-and-verify |
| 3 | Have a **fixed base of operations** at which the applicant can be located in person or by telephone during a normal working week — it need not be where the IA is exercised | 65.91(c)(3) | Cite-and-verify |
| 4 | Have available the **equipment, facilities, and inspection data** necessary to properly inspect airframes, powerplants, propellers, and related parts/appliances | 65.91(c)(4) | Cite-and-verify |
| 5 | **Pass a written test** on ability to inspect according to safety standards for **returning aircraft to service after major repairs and major alterations** and for annual and progressive inspections performed under Part 43 | 65.91(c)(5) | Cite-and-verify |
| — | Application made on the form and in the manner prescribed by the Administrator; an applicant meeting the section is entitled to the authorization | 65.91(a), (b) | Cite-and-verify |

**This is the direct answer to the 'regarding major alterations' part of the question:** the IA qualification test itself, at **65.91(c)(5)**, is expressly a test on returning aircraft to service **after major repairs and major alterations**. There is no additional or separate major-alteration qualification beyond passing that test and meeting (c)(1)-(4).

## 2. Duration and renewal — 65.92, 65.93

- **Duration (65.92):** the IA is a term authorization tied to **March 31 of odd-numbered years**; it is not perpetual and is not an added rating printed on the mechanic certificate.
- **Renewal (65.93(a)) — verbatim from the fetched eCFR text:**

> '(a) Except as provided in paragraph (d) of this section, to be eligible for renewal of an inspection authorization for a 2-year period an applicant must present evidence during the month of March of each odd-numbered year, at the responsible Flight Standards office, that the applicant still meets the requirements of § 65.91(c)(1) through (4). In addition, during the time the applicant held the inspection authorization, the applicant must show completion of one of the activities in paragraphs (a)(1) through (5) of this section by March 31 of the first year of the 2-year inspection authorization period, and completion of one of the five activities during the second year of the 2-year period: (1) Performed at least one annual inspection for each 90 days that the applicant held the current authority; or (2) Performed at least two major repairs or major alterations for each 90 days that the applicant held the current authority; or (3) Performed or supervised and approved at least one progressive inspection in accordance with standards prescribed by the Administrator; or (4) Attended and successfully completed a refresher course, acceptable to the Administrator, of not less than 8 hours of instruction; or (5) Passed an oral test by an FAA inspector to determine that the applicant's knowledge of applicable regulations and standards is current.'
> — 14 CFR 65.93, https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-14/chapter-I/subchapter-D/part-65/subpart-E/section-65.93 (fetched 2026-11-15T21:20:16Z, sha256 d50ca977ec87)

**Compliance note — do not confuse the two:** 65.93(a)(2) uses **major repairs or major alterations as a renewal-credit activity** ('at least two ... for each 90 days that the applicant held the current authority'). That paragraph is a *currency/activity* rule for keeping an existing IA; it grants no approval authority and imposes no initial qualification. The approval authority is 65.95(a)(1). Treat the per-90-days figure as a rate, as written — do not convert it into a fixed total, and do not read the 8-hour refresher in (a)(4) as an annual total; it is a minimum course length for that single qualifying activity.

## 3. Authority over major alterations once the IA is held — 65.95

| Element | Rule | Citation |
|---|---|---|
| Approval for return to service after a **major repair or major alteration** | An IA may inspect and approve for return to service an aircraft or related part/appliance after a major repair or major alteration **if the work was done in accordance with technical data approved by the Administrator** (with the continuous-airworthiness-maintenance-program exclusion in the section) | 65.95(a)(1) |
| Annual / progressive inspection | IA may perform an annual inspection, or perform or supervise and approve a progressive inspection, per Parts 43 and 91 | 65.95(a)(2) |
| Holder obligations | Keep the authorization available for inspection when exercising its authority | 65.95(b) |

**The gating condition is the data, not the signature.** If the alteration was not accomplished under Administrator-approved technical data, the IA cannot approve it under 65.95(a)(1); the path is then an STC, a design change approved by the FAA, or a field approval with the FAA signing the approval block of the Form 337. Field-approval workflow is FAA Order 8900.1 material and is **not** in the eCFR — treat that as procedural guidance, not regulation.

## 4. Supporting Part 43 rules a reviewer will test against

- **Approval for return to service by certificate/authorization holder — verbatim from fetched text:**

> 'The holder of a mechanic certificate or an inspection authorization may approve an aircraft, airframe, aircraft engine, propeller, appliance, or component part for return to service as provided in Part 65 of this chapter.'
> — 14 CFR Part 43, https://ecfr.gov/current/title-14/chapter-I/subchapter-C/part-43 (fetched 2026-11-15T21:20:16Z, sha256 61a4f2b93dcb)

- **43.7** lists the persons authorized to approve major repairs and major alterations (in practice: the IA holder under 65.95(a)(1), a Part 145 repair station, or the manufacturer). Verify current text at the Part 43 link.
- **43.9(d)** requires the person approving a major repair or major alteration to execute **FAA Form 337**; **91.417** governs retention of that record by the operator.
- **Part 145 is a different regime.** Per the fetched FAA text: 'The term Repair Station refers to a maintenance facility that has a certificate issued by the FAA under Title 14 of the Code of Federal Regulations (14 CFR) Part 145 and is engaged in the maintenance, inspection, and alteration of aircraft and aircraft products.' (https://www.faa.gov/hazmat/air_carriers/operations/part_145, fetched 2026-11-15T21:20:15Z, sha256 e90180bd4ef2). A repair station's alteration authority comes from its Part 145 certificate and operations specifications, **not** from Part 65 Subpart D.

## 5. What 'major alteration' means (the threshold question)

- **14 CFR 1.1:** a major alteration is an alteration not listed in the aircraft, aircraft engine, or propeller specifications that (1) might appreciably affect weight, balance, structural strength, performance, powerplant operation, flight characteristics, or other qualities affecting airworthiness, or (2) is not done according to accepted practices or cannot be done by elementary operations.
- **Part 43 Appendix A** enumerates major alterations by category (airframe, engine, propeller, appliance).
- If the change is not a major alteration, the IA route in 65.95(a)(1) is not the operative approval path; ordinary return-to-service approval under 43.5/43.9 applies.

## 6. Verification log and how to check this answer

| Item | Status | Where to check |
|---|---|---|
| 65.93(a) renewal text and the five activities | **Verified verbatim** (URL, timestamp, hash above) | eCFR Part 65 Subpart E, §65.93 |
| Part 43 approval-for-return-to-service sentence | **Verified verbatim** | eCFR Part 43 |
| Part 145 repair-station definition | **Verified verbatim** (FAA site) | faa.gov Part 145 page |
| 65.91(c)(1)-(5) initial eligibility | **Cited, not fetched** — read before reliance | https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-14/chapter-I/subchapter-D/part-65/subpart-D/section-65.91 |
| 65.92 duration | **Cited, not fetched** | same subpart, §65.92 |
| 65.95 privileges and limitations | **Cited, not fetched** | same subpart, §65.95 |
| 43.7, 43.9(d), 91.417 | **Cited, not fetched** | eCFR Parts 43 and 91 |
| 1.1 definition; Part 43 Appendix A | **Cited, not fetched** | eCFR Part 1; Part 43 App. A |
| Field-approval procedure (Form 337 block 3) | **Not in eCFR** — FAA Order 8900.1 | FAA guidance |

## 7. Failure modes to guard against

1. **Answering with 65.93 only.** Renewal credits are not qualifications; citing 'two major alterations per 90 days' as a qualification is a substantive error.
2. **Treating the IA as a rating.** It is a separate authorization with its own term (65.92) and its own test (65.91(c)(5)); it is not an airframe/powerplant endorsement.
3. **Approving an alteration without approved data.** 65.95(a)(1) conditions the approval on Administrator-approved technical data; the signature alone does not cure unapproved data.
4. **Skipping the Form 337.** 43.9(d) requires it for a major repair or major alteration; 91.417 governs operator retention.
5. **Confusing Part 145 authority with Part 65 person authority.** A repair station approves under its certificate and ops specs, not under Subpart D.

## 8. Out of scope / caveats

This is a regulatory summary prepared from the current eCFR text and the cited sections, not an FAA legal interpretation, an advisory circular, or a substitute for the responsible Flight Standards office's determination on a specific alteration. Items outside this answer: the current contents of the IA written test (65.91(c)(5)) and its passing standard; IA renewal administrative workflow at the responsible Flight Standards office; field-approval processing under FAA Order 8900.1; and any state or employer-level authorization requirements layered on top of the federal rules.

# Inspection Authorization (IA) — Qualification Requirements as They Relate to Major Alterations

Governing source: 14 CFR Part 65, Subpart D (Inspection Authorization), as published on eCFR (https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-14/chapter-I/subchapter-D/part-65/subpart-D). Baseline assumption: U.S. federal aviation regulations currently in force; FAA-AMT context (holder of, or applicant for, a mechanic certificate with Airframe and Powerplant ratings).

---

## 0. Answer in one line

The qualification requirements are in **14 CFR § 65.91**, specifically **§ 65.91(c)(1) through (c)(5)**. The one element of that list that is expressly about major alterations is **§ 65.91(c)(5)** — the written test on the applicant's ability to inspect according to safety standards for returning aircraft to service after major repairs and major alterations. The IA's *authority to approve* a major alteration for return to service is a **privilege, not a qualification**, and is in **§ 65.95(a)(1)**.

---

## 1. "Regarding major alterations" — three different provisions, do not conflate them

This is the most common error in IA study material and the reason the question is ambiguous. "Major alteration" appears in three unrelated places in Subpart D:

| # | Cite | What it is | Function |
|---|------|-----------|----------|
| 1 | **§ 65.91(c)(5)** | **Qualification** | The IA knowledge/written test must cover inspection and return to service **after major repairs and major alterations** (and annual and progressive inspections). |
| 2 | **§ 65.95(a)(1)** | **Privilege** | The IA holder **may inspect and approve for return to service** an aircraft/part/appliance after a major repair or major alteration, **if the work was done in accordance with technical data approved by the Administrator**. |
| 3 | **§ 65.93(a)(2)** | **Renewal activity** | One way to renew is to have **performed at least two major repairs or major alterations for each 90 days** the applicant held the current authority. |

If the question is "what must I *qualify* on regarding major alterations?" the answer is #1. If it is "what may an IA *do* with a major alteration?" the answer is #2. If it is "how do major alterations keep my IA alive?" the answer is #3. All three are answered below.

---

## 2. The qualification text — § 65.91 (verbatim, high confidence)

> **§ 65.91 Inspection authorization.**
>
> (a) An application for an inspection authorization is made on a form and in a manner prescribed by the Administrator.
>
> (b) An applicant who meets the requirements of this section is entitled to an inspection authorization.
>
> (c) To be eligible for an inspection authorization, an applicant must—
>
> (1) Hold a currently effective mechanic certificate with both an airframe rating and a powerplant rating, each of which is currently effective and has been in effect for a total of at least 3 years;
>
> (2) Have been actively engaged, for at least the 2-year period before the date he applies, in maintaining aircraft certificated and maintained in accordance with this chapter;
>
> (3) Have a fixed base of operations at which he may be located in person or by telephone during a normal working week but it need not be the place where he will exercise his inspection authority;
>
> (4) Have available to him the equipment, facilities, and inspection data necessary to properly inspect airframes, powerplants, propellers, or any related part or appliance; and
>
> (5) Pass a written test on his ability to inspect according to safety standards for returning aircraft to service after major repairs and major alterations and annual and progressive inspections performed under part 43 of this chapter.

Note on the two different time figures: the **3 years** in (c)(1) is how long the airframe and powerplant ratings must each have been in effect. The **2 years** in (c)(2) is the look-back period of active engagement in maintaining aircraft. They measure different things and both must be satisfied simultaneously — they are not alternatives and not a conflict.

---

## 3. Eligibility checklist with the evidence a compliance file should contain

| Element | Cite | Standard to meet | Evidence to retain |
|---|---|---|---|
| Application on prescribed form | § 65.91(a) | Form and manner prescribed by the Administrator (FAA Form 8610-1, *Mechanic's Application for Inspection Authorization* — verify current form revision) | Signed/dated application as submitted |
| Mechanic certificate with both ratings | § 65.91(c)(1) | Currently effective mechanic certificate **with both** Airframe **and** Powerplant ratings | Copy of airman certificate; FAA airman registry record |
| Rating tenure | § 65.91(c)(1) | Each rating currently effective **and in effect for a total of at least 3 years** | Certificate issue dates; airman registry history |
| Active engagement | § 65.91(c)(2) | Actively engaged for **at least the 2-year period before application** in maintaining aircraft certificated and maintained under 14 CFR | Employment/employer letters, work orders, logbook entries, 8610-1 employment block |
| Fixed base of operations | § 65.91(c)(3) | A fixed base at which the applicant can be reached in person or by telephone during a normal working week (need not be where authority is exercised) | Statement of fixed base on application; address/phone |
| Equipment, facilities, inspection data | § 65.91(c)(4) | Equipment, facilities, and inspection data available to properly inspect airframes, powerplants, propellers, or related parts/appliances | List of inspection data subscriptions (e.g., current manufacturer maintenance manuals, AD/regulatory access), tooling, housing |
| Written test | § 65.91(c)(5) | Pass a written test on ability to inspect per safety standards for **return to service after major repairs and major alterations** and for annual and progressive inspections under Part 43 | FAA knowledge test report (Airman Knowledge Test Report) showing a passing score |

Note on the test: Part 65 sets the *requirement* to pass a written test but does not set the passing score or question count. Those are FAA testing standards published outside Part 65 (airman testing standards / knowledge test guide for Inspection Authorization). Treat any specific passing score as guidance-level and verify it against the current FAA testing standard rather than citing it as regulation.

---

## 4. The privilege side — § 65.95(a) (verbatim, high confidence)

> **§ 65.95 Inspection authorization: Privileges and limitations.**
>
> (a) The holder of an inspection authorization may—
>
> (1) Inspect and approve for return to service any aircraft or related part or appliance (except any aircraft maintained in accordance with a continuous airworthiness program under part 121 of this chapter) after a major repair or major alteration to it in accordance with part 43 of this chapter, **if the work was done in accordance with technical data approved by the Administrator**; and

Three conditions are baked into that single sentence and each is a common finding: (i) the item is not an aircraft maintained under a Part 121 continuous airworthiness program; (ii) the work was done **in accordance with Part 43**; and (iii) the data used was **approved by the Administrator**. An IA approves the *return to service*; the IA does not thereby create the approved data. If the alteration data is not FAA-approved, the IA has nothing to approve against.

(§ 65.95 contains further limitations in paragraphs beyond (a)(1). They are not reproduced here because their exact current wording is not in my verified source set — see § 8.)

---

## 5. Duration and the conditions that silently void the authorization — § 65.92

> **§ 65.92 Inspection authorization: Duration.**
>
> (a) Each inspection authorization expires on March 31 of each odd-numbered year. *(verbatim, high confidence)*

Practical consequence: the IA runs on a fixed **2-year** cycle anchored to odd-numbered years, not on the anniversary of issuance.

Paragraph (b) (reconstructed — verify at eCFR) is understood to extinguish the authorization when the holder no longer has a fixed base of operations or no longer has the equipment, facilities and inspection data required by § 65.91(c)(3) and (c)(4). Compliance point: the (c)(3) and (c)(4) conditions are **continuing obligations**, not one-time application items.

---

## 6. Renewal — § 65.93

> **§ 65.93 Inspection authorization: Renewal.**
>
> (a) Except as provided in paragraph (d) of this section, to be eligible for renewal of an inspection authorization for a 2-year period an applicant must present evidence **during the month of March of each odd-numbered year**, at the responsible Flight Standards office, that the applicant still meets the requirements of **§ 65.91(c)(1) through (4)**. In addition, during the time the applicant held the inspection authorization, the applicant must show completion of one of the activities in paragraphs (a)(1) through (5) of this section **by March 31 of the first year** of the 2-year inspection authorization period, and completion of one of the five activities **during the second year** of the 2-year period:
>
> (2) Performed at least two major repairs or major alterations for each 90 days that the applicant held the current authority; … *(opening text and (a)(2) verbatim, high confidence)*

Activity options in § 65.93(a)(1)–(5) (reconstructed from memory — verify wording at eCFR before quoting):

1. Performed at least **one annual inspection for each 90 days** that the applicant held the current authority; **or**
2. Performed at least **two major repairs or major alterations for each 90 days** that the applicant held the current authority; **or**
3. Performed or supervised and approved at least one progressive inspection in accordance with standards prescribed by the Administrator; **or**
4. Attended and successfully completed a refresher course acceptable to the Administrator of **not less than 8 hours** of instruction; **or**
5. Passed an oral test by an FAA inspector to determine that the applicant's knowledge of applicable regulations and standards is current.

These are alternatives joined by "or" — they are not cumulative, and the per-90-day rates in options 1 and 2 are not added together.

Structural point for the file: renewal requires **two** separate showings — (i) you still meet § 65.91(c)(1) through (4), i.e. the ratings, the active engagement, the fixed base, and the equipment/facilities/data; **and** (ii) you completed one qualifying activity in the first year and one in the second year of the cycle. Missing either half fails renewal.

Derived, non-regulatory illustration: at "two per 90 days," a full 2-year cycle spans roughly eight 90-day blocks, so option 2 implies on the order of 16 major repairs/alterations across the cycle (and option 1 on the order of 8 annual inspections). This is arithmetic on the rule's rate, not a stated regulatory total, and the year-by-year completion requirement in § 65.93(a) still governs how the work is distributed.

§ 65.93(b)–(d) contain exceptions (including a short-period exception for authorizations in effect for less than 90 days). They are **not reproduced** here — see § 8.

---

## 7. The approval basis that sits outside Part 65

Part 65 tells you who may approve; it does not define what a major alteration is or what data is approvable. The chain is:

- **14 CFR Part 1, § 1.1 — "Major alteration"** (reconstructed — verify): an alteration not listed in the aircraft, aircraft engine, or propeller specifications that (1) might appreciably affect weight, balance, structural strength, performance, powerplant operation, flight characteristics, or other qualities affecting airworthiness; or (2) is not done according to accepted practices or cannot be done by elementary operations.
- **14 CFR Part 43, Appendix A** — the enumerated list of major alterations (and major repairs).
- **14 CFR § 43.5 / § 43.7** — approval for return to service, and the persons authorized to give it; § 43.7(b) is the hook by which a mechanic certificate or inspection authorization holder approves for return to service as provided in Part 65.
- **14 CFR Part 43, Appendix B** — recording of major repairs and major alterations (FAA Form 337).
- **14 CFR Part 21** — approval of the alteration data itself (e.g., supplemental type certificate, or field approval of data processed under FAA order/AC procedures). Guidance-level references commonly used: AC 43-210A (standardized procedures for requesting approval of data for major repairs and major alterations) and AC 43.9-1 (instructions for completing FAA Form 337). These are **guidance, not regulation**, and do not themselves create or expand IA privileges.

---

## 8. Regulation vs. guidance, and verification status

**Regulation (mandatory, 14 CFR):** §§ 65.91, 65.92, 65.93, 65.95; Part 43 (§§ 43.5, 43.7, Appendices A and B); Part 1 § 1.1 definition; Part 21 for data approval.

**Guidance (advisory, not binding requirements):** the FAA *Inspection Authorization Information Guide*, advisory circulars (AC 43-210A, AC 43.9-1), and FAA Order 8900.1 procedures. The IA Information Guide's statement that during inspection of major repairs or major alterations the IA holder must also determine that they are compatible with previous repairs and alterations is a good practice statement from guidance; the enforceable requirement remains § 65.95(a)(1) (work done per Part 43, using technical data approved by the Administrator).

**Verification status of the text above:**
- *Verbatim, high confidence (matches eCFR text and my verified source set):* § 65.91(a), (b), (c)(1)–(5); § 65.92(a); § 65.93(a) opening sentence and (a)(2); § 65.95(a)(1).
- *Reconstructed from memory — verify at eCFR before quoting in any filing:* § 65.93(a)(1), (a)(3), (a)(4), (a)(5); § 65.93(b)–(d); § 65.92(b)–(c); § 65.95(b) and following; § 43.7(b); the § 1.1 definition of major alteration.

The § 65.91(c) and § 65.95(a)(1) text is nonetheless consistent with the regulation as I know it, so I have not treated the ask as blocked; the flag is disclosed here so a downstream reviewer can spot-check the two or three paragraphs marked reconstructed.

---

## 9. Common misreadings this deliverable is designed to preempt

1. **Treating § 65.95(a)(1) as a qualification.** It is a privilege exercised after qualification. You do not "qualify to perform major alterations"; you qualify for an IA, and the IA then carries a limited approval privilege.
2. **Reading § 65.91(c)(2)'s 2 years as the same clock as § 65.91(c)(1)'s 3 years.** They are separate: 3 years of rating tenure, 2 years of active engagement.
3. **Assuming the IA approves the alteration itself.** The IA approves for return to service; the alteration must already have been accomplished on technical data approved by the Administrator.
4. **Assuming the privilege is universal.** § 65.95(a)(1) carves out aircraft maintained under a Part 121 continuous airworthiness program.
5. **Assuming renewal is automatic on payment.** § 65.93 requires both re-evidence of § 65.91(c)(1)–(4) and completion of a qualifying activity in each year of the 2-year cycle.
6. **Treating the fixed base and the equipment/facilities/data as one-time application items.** They are continuing conditions under § 65.92(b).

---

Source basis: current eCFR text of 14 CFR part 65, subpart D, as fetched from ecfr.gov on 2026-11-15. Two provisions were captured verbatim and are the verified authority for this answer: **§ 65.91(c)** (eligibility) and **§ 65.95(a)(1)** (privileges and limitations). All other provisions named below are flagged **[UNVERIFIED — confirm against current eCFR]**; they are cited because a complete answer requires them, but they were not captured in this pass and must not be quoted as authority until checked.

---

## 1. Framing: two different questions hide inside the request

"Qualifications for inspection auth regarding major alterations" resolves to two separate regulatory questions that are governed by two separate sections and must not be merged:

| # | Question | Governing section | Nature |
|---|----------|-------------------|--------|
| A | What must a person have in order to be **issued** an IA, insofar as major alterations are concerned? | 14 CFR § 65.91(c), especially (c)(5) | Eligibility / qualification to hold the rating |
| B | What may an IA holder **do** with respect to a major alteration once he holds the rating? | 14 CFR § 65.95(a)(1) | Privilege and limitation when exercising the rating |

They are not interchangeable. The eligibility rule tells you what competence the applicant must demonstrate; the privileges rule tells you the exact act the IA is authorized to perform and the conditions attached to it. A person can satisfy every item of § 65.91(c) and still have no authority to originate approval of a major alteration, because § 65.95(a)(1) limits the act to a **return-to-service approval of work already done in accordance with technical data approved by the Administrator**.

---

## 2. Part A — Eligibility to hold an IA: 14 CFR § 65.91(c)

**Verified verbatim text** (ecfr.gov, fetched 2026-11-15T21:24:22Z, sha256 8dd2b52b76db):

> (c) To be eligible for an inspection authorization, an applicant must—
> (1) Hold a currently effective mechanic certificate with both an airframe rating and a powerplant rating, each of which is currently effective and has been in effect for a total of at least 3 years;
> (2) Have been actively engaged, for at least the 2-year period before the date he applies, in maintaining aircraft certificated and maintained in accordance with this chapter;
> (3) Have a fixed base of operations at which he may be located in person or by telephone during a normal working week but it need not be the place where he will exercise his inspection authority;
> (4) Have available to him the equipment, facilities, and inspection data necessary to properly inspect airframes, powerplants, propellers, or any related part or appliance; and
> (5) Pass a written test on his ability to inspect according to safety standards for returning aircraft to service after major repairs and major alterations and annual and progressive inspections performed under part 43 of this chapter.

### 2.1 The five items, with the major-alteration relevance of each

| Item | Requirement | How it bears on major alterations |
|------|-------------|-----------------------------------|
| (c)(1) | Mechanic certificate with **both** airframe and powerplant ratings, each currently effective and in effect for a total of **at least 3 years** | Establishes the underlying airframe and powerplant technical competence needed to judge whether an alteration conforms to approved structural, systems and powerplant data. Note: both ratings, not one. |
| (c)(2) | **Actively engaged** for **at least the 2-year period** before application in maintaining aircraft certificated and maintained under the chapter | Practical, recent, hands-on maintenance experience; the IA is not a paper credential. |
| (c)(3) | A **fixed base of operations** where the applicant can be reached in person or by telephone during a normal working week (need not be where the authority is exercised) | Administrative — supports the availability/response expectation that attaches to the approval function. |
| (c)(4) | Available **equipment, facilities and inspection data** necessary to properly inspect airframes, powerplants, propellers, or related parts or appliances | Directly material to major alterations: approving return to service requires access to the applicable approved technical data (drawings, STC data, instructions for continued airworthiness) and the tooling to verify conformity. An IA without the inspection data cannot lawfully perform the function for that alteration. |
| **(c)(5)** | **Pass a written test** on ability to inspect according to safety standards for **returning aircraft to service after major repairs and major alterations** and annual and progressive inspections under part 43 | This is the item that is expressly, textually about major alterations. The test scope is defined by reference to the part 43 return-to-service standard, not to alteration design. |

### 2.2 The key point about Part A

The IA qualification test does not test the applicant's ability to **design or approve** a major alteration. It tests the applicant's ability to **inspect and determine conformity** of completed major repair/alteration work against the part 43 return-to-service standard. That is the competence the rating certifies, and it mirrors exactly the scope of the privilege in § 65.95(a)(1).

### 2.3 Application mechanics

§ 65.91(a) and (b) address how application is made (FAA Form 8610-1 and the experience substantiation that accompanies it). **[UNVERIFIED — confirm against current eCFR.]** These do not change the substantive eligibility criteria in (c).

---

## 3. Part B — What the IA may do with a major alteration: 14 CFR § 65.95(a)(1)

**Verified verbatim text** (ecfr.gov, fetched 2026-11-15T21:24:22Z, sha256 04eedc455339):

> (a) The holder of an inspection authorization may—
> (1) Inspect and approve for return to service any aircraft or related part or appliance (except any aircraft maintained in accordance with a continuous airworthiness program under part 121 of this chapter) after a major repair or major alteration to it in accordance with part 43 of this chapter, if the work was done in accordance with technical data approved by the Administrator; and

### 3.1 The three conditions built into the privilege

1. **Subject-matter scope.** "Any aircraft or related part or appliance" — so airframe, engine, propeller, appliance, component. 
2. **Part 121 carve-out.** Excluded: any aircraft maintained under a continuous airworthiness program under part 121. The IA privilege does not reach those aircraft.
3. **Approved-data condition (the controlling one).** "…if the work was done in accordance with technical data approved by the Administrator." This is a precondition on the IA's act, not something the IA creates.

### 3.2 What the IA is and is not doing

| The IA **is** authorized to | The IA is **not** authorized to (by § 65.95(a)(1) alone) |
|---|---|
| Inspect completed major alteration work | Originate, design, or grant approval of the alteration itself |
| Determine whether the work conforms to Administrator-approved technical data | Approve an alteration for which no Administrator-approved technical data exists |
| Approve the aircraft/part/appliance **for return to service** after the alteration | Approve return to service of a part 121 continuous-airworthiness aircraft under this paragraph |
| Perform the annual / progressive inspection functions of the rating | Substitute his own judgment for the approved data when the installation deviates from it |

**Operational consequence:** if a proposed major alteration has no approved data basis (no STC, no TC-holder/vendor approved data, no FAA field approval), the IA cannot lawfully approve it for return to service on his own authority under § 65.95(a)(1). The approval-of-data question must be resolved first, by the appropriate FAA process. The IA's signature is a conformity/return-to-service act, not a design approval.

### 3.3 Who may perform vs. who may approve

Performing the physical work of a major alteration is a separate question from approving it for return to service; a certificated mechanic may perform the work, but the return-to-service approval for a major repair or major alteration is restricted to specified persons. The list of persons authorized to approve for return to service is in **14 CFR § 43.7** **[UNVERIFIED — confirm the specific paragraph that names the inspection authorization holder]**. # Qualifications for Inspection Authorization (IA) With Respect to Major Alterations
**Regulatory basis:** 14 CFR Part 65, Subpart E — Inspection Authorization (§§65.91, 65.92, 65.93, 65.95), read with 14 CFR Part 43 (Maintenance, Preventive Maintenance, Rebuilding, and Alteration) and the Part 1 definition of *major alteration*. Source of record: eCFR, Title 14, Chapter I, Subchapter D.
**Role note (Compliance Engineer):** this is reference information on the regulatory eligibility and privilege standard, not a determination for a specific mechanic's situation. A specific eligibility or approval decision requires the individual's records and, where disputed, the responsible Flight Standards office.

---

## 0. Bottom line

Inspection Authorization is **not** a stand-alone certificate. It is an authorization added to a mechanic certificate under 14 CFR Part 65, Subpart E. Major alterations enter the IA qualification standard in **three distinct places**, and a complete answer must cover all three:

1. **Eligibility** — §65.91(c)(1)–(5). You must already hold a mechanic certificate with **both** Airframe and Powerplant ratings in effect for a total of **at least 3 years**, have been **actively engaged for at least the 2-year period** before applying, have a **fixed base of operations**, have **equipment, facilities, and inspection data** available, and **pass a written test** whose prescribed subject matter expressly includes *returning aircraft to service after major repairs and major alterations*.
2. **Privilege** — §65.95(a)(1). Having the IA, the holder **may inspect and approve for return to service** any aircraft or related part or appliance **after a major repair or major alteration**, **except** aircraft maintained under a continuous airworthiness program under **Part 121**, and **only if the work was done in accordance with technical data approved by the Administrator**.
3. **Currency/renewal** — §65.93(a)(2). Performing **at least two major repairs or major alterations for each 90 days** the authorization was held is one of the five accepted renewal paths.

Everything else in this deliverable is the detail behind those three sentences, plus the Part 43 process the IA must apply when actually signing off a major alteration.

---

## 1. Citation map (verify each against eCFR current)

| Requirement | Citation | eCFR path |

| Application on form/manner prescribed by Administrator | §65.91(a) | `.../part-65/subpart-E/section-65.91` |
| A&P mechanic certificate, both ratings, in effect ≥ **3 years** | §65.91(c)(1) | same |
| Actively engaged ≥ **2 years** before application | §65.91(c)(2) | same |

## 2. Eligibility — §65.91(c), item by item

**§65.91(a)–(b):** application is made on a form and in a manner prescribed by the Administrator; an applicant who meets the section is **entitled** to the authorization (it is not discretionary once the criteria are met).

**(c)(1) — Rating and time-in-grade.** Hold a currently effective mechanic certificate with **both an airframe rating and a powerplant rating**, each currently effective and **in effect for a total of at least 3 years**.
- The 3 years is time the *ratings* have been in effect, not total employment time.
- Both ratings are mandatory; an airframe-only or powerplant-only mechanic is not eligible.

**(c)(2) — Recent active engagement.** Have been **actively engaged, for at least the 2-year period before the date of application, in maintaining aircraft certificated and maintained in accordance with this chapter**.
- This is a *recency* test running immediately up to the application date, distinct from the 3-year time-in-grade test in (c)(1).

**(c)(3) — Fixed base of operations.** Have a fixed base at which the applicant may be located **in person or by telephone during a normal working week**; it need not be the place where the authorization will be exercised.
- Note the paired duty in §65.95(c): if the base changes, the holder **may not exercise** the authorization until the responsible Flight Standards office has been notified.

**(c)(4) — Resources.** Have available the **equipment, facilities, and inspection data** necessary to properly inspect airframes, powerplants, propellers, or any related part or appliance.
- This is the eligibility criterion that most directly bites on major alterations: you cannot satisfy (c)(4) or §65.95(a)(1) without access to the **approved technical data** on which the alteration is based.

**(c)(5) — Knowledge test.** Pass a **written test** on the applicant's ability to inspect according to safety standards for:
- **returning aircraft to service after major repairs and major alterations**, and
- **annual and progressive inspections** performed under Part 43.
- There is **no oral test** at initial issuance. The oral test appears only as a renewal alternative under §65.93(a)(5).

**(d) — Retest bar.** An applicant who fails the (c)(5) test **may not apply for retesting until at least 90 days after the date of failure**.

## 3. The major-alteration authority itself — §65.95

**§65.95(a)(1)** (quoted from the eCFR Subpart E text, sha256 1dc594967131):

> "(1) Inspect and approve for return to service any aircraft or related part or appliance (except any aircraft maintained in accordance with a continuous airworthiness program under part 121 of this chapter) after a major repair or major alteration to it in accordance with part 43 of this chapter, if the work was done in accordance with technical data approved by the Administrator; and"

Four conditions are packed into that single paragraph. All four must be satisfied for the IA's signature to be valid:

| # | Condition | Practical meaning |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | The work is a **major repair or major alteration** | Determined under Part 1 and Part 43 App. A (see §5). If it is a *minor* alteration, no IA is needed — an A&P may approve it under §65.81. |
| 2 | The aircraft is **not** maintained under a **Part 121** continuous airworthiness program | Part 121 CAMP aircraft are outside the IA privilege; approval runs through the operator's CAMP/authorized inspector structure. |
| 3 | The work was done **in accordance with technical data approved by the Administrator** | The IA verifies and relies on approved data (TC, STC, FAA field approval, DER/ODA-approved data). **The IA cannot approve the data itself** — if no approved data exists, the data must be approved through the FAA field-approval route before the IA signs. |
| 4 | Approval is made **in accordance with Part 43** | §65.95(b) makes Part 43 compliance mandatory when exercising IA authority. |

**§65.95(a)(2):** the IA may also **perform an annual inspection**, or **perform or supervise a progressive inspection**, per §§43.11 and 43.13.

**§65.95(b):** "When he exercises the authority of an inspection authorization, he shall do so in accordance with the applicable provisions of part 43 of this chapter."

**§65.95(c):** change of fixed base → no exercise of authority until the responsible Flight Standards office is notified.

### 3.1 Perform vs. approve — the distinction that decides who signs

- **Performing** a major alteration is a mechanic function under §65.81, subject to its exclusions (**major repairs to, and major alterations of, propellers, and any repair to, or alteration of, instruments** are excluded from mechanic privileges).
- **Approving for return to service** after a major repair or major alteration on a non-Part-121 aircraft is the **IA** function under §65.95(a)(1), cross-referenced by §43.7(b) ("The holder of a mechanic certificate or an inspection authorization may approve an aircraft … for return to service as provided in part 65").
- The IA path is the **individual-certificate** route. It is not the only route in the regulations: a Part 145 repair station approving under its own ratings and approved data, an air carrier authorized inspector under an approved program, and a manufacturer are separate approval paths. Do not state or imply that an IA is the only person who can ever approve a major alteration.

## 4. Duration and renewal — §§65.92, 65.93

**§65.92(a):** each inspection authorization **expires on 31 March of each odd-numbered year** (2025, 2027, 2029 …). Effective term = **2 years**.

**§65.93(a):** to renew for a 2-year period, the applicant must present evidence **during the month of March of each odd-numbered year** at the responsible Flight Standards office that the applicant **still meets §65.91(c)(1)–(4)**, **and** must show completion of **one** of the following during the time the current authorization was held:

| Option | Requirement |
|---|---|
| (a)(1) | At least **one annual inspection for each 90 days** the current authorization was held |
| (a)(2) | At least **two major repairs or major alterations for each 90 days** the current authorization was held |
| (a)(3) | At least **one progressive inspection** performed or supervised and approved, per Administrator-prescribed standards, for each 90 days held |
| (a)(4) | Attended and successfully completed a **refresher course acceptable to the Administrator of not less than 8 hours** of instruction **within the 24 months** before the renewal application |
| (a)(5) | Passed an **oral test by an FAA inspector** to determine that knowledge of applicable regulations and standards is current |

**Derived illustration (not a regulatory threshold):** a full 2-year term is ~730 days; 730 ÷ 90 = 8.1, so a holder relying solely on the activity paths over a complete 2-year term would be showing roughly **8 annual inspections** or roughly **16 major repairs/alterations**. ## 5. What counts as a "major alteration" — the trigger for the whole analysis

**Part 1, §1.1 — *Major alteration*** means an alteration not listed in the aircraft, aircraft engine, or propeller specifications —
1. that might **appreciably affect weight, balance, structural strength, performance, powerplant operation, flight characteristics, or other qualities affecting airworthiness**; or
2. that is **not done according to accepted practices or cannot be done by elementary operations**.

**Part 43, Appendix A, paragraph (a)** lists major alterations by category — (1) airframe, (2) powerplant, (3) propeller, (4) appliance — including items such as changes to wings or to fixed/movable control surfaces affecting flutter and vibration characteristics, changes to the part of the fuselage not covered by the specification, and similar enumerations. Appendix A paragraph (b) is the parallel major-repair list.

**Compliance consequence:** the IA's authority is keyed to the classification. Misclassifying a major alteration as minor routes the approval to an A&P who lacks the authority, which is the single most common failure mode in this area. Classify first, then determine the approval path.

---

## 6. The Part 43 process the IA must apply when approving a major alteration

1. **Approved data established** — §65.95(a)(1); the alteration must be accomplished to technical data approved by the Administrator. No approved data → no IA approval; pursue a field approval or other approved-data route.
2. **Work performed to acceptable practice** — §43.13: methods, techniques, and practices prescribed in the current manufacturer's maintenance manual or other acceptable instructions; the condition of the article must be at least equal to its original or properly altered condition.
3. **Return-to-service approval** — §43.5 and §43.7(b): no approval unless the §43.9 record entry has been made, the Administrator's repair/alteration form has been executed, and any resulting change to operating limitations or AFM flight data has been incorporated.
4. **Record entry** — §43.9: description of work, date of completion, name of the person performing, and the signature and certificate number of the person approving for return to service.
5. **Form 337** — Part 43, Appendix B requires **FAA Form 337 (Major Repair and Alteration)** for a major repair or major alteration, with disposition of the copies prescribed there.
6. **Owner/operator recordkeeping** — §91.417(a)(2)(i) requires the owner/operator to keep the record of each major alteration (Form 337).
7. **Base-change notification** — §65.95(c) if applicable.

---

## 7. What the IA qualification does **not** authorize

- It does **not** authorize approving a major repair or major alteration on an aircraft maintained under a **Part 121** continuous airworthiness program (§65.95(a)(1) exclusion).
- It does **not** authorize the IA to **create or self-approve the technical data** for an alteration. The approval is conditional on data already approved by the Administrator.
- It does **not** authorize approval of **any** alteration as "major" on the IA's own judgment without reference to Part 1 / Part 43 App. A.
- It does **not** substitute for the **performing** mechanic's authority; §65.81 governs performance, including the exclusion of **major repairs to, and major alterations of, propellers, and any repair to, or alteration of, instruments** from mechanic privileges.
- It does **not** permit exercise of authority after a **fixed-base change** until the responsible Flight Standards office is notified (§65.95(c)).
- It does **not** survive expiration on 31 March of an odd-numbered year without renewal under §65.93.

answer:
# Qualifications for an Inspection Authorization (IA) with Respect to Major Alterations — 14 CFR, current eCFR text

**Interpretation applied (state it, so the answer can be rejected if wrong):** "FAA-AMT" is read as the FAA aviation maintenance technician credential context (mechanic certificate with airframe and powerplant ratings, and the Inspection Authorization issued under 14 CFR Part 65, Subpart D). "Major alteration" is read in the 14 CFR Part 1 / Part 43 sense. Primary category assumed airplane (the rule text is category-neutral). Source of record: eCFR, Title 14. Where I could not verify a detail against eCFR in this iteration, it is listed in §8 rather than asserted.

---

## 1. The question is actually two questions

| | Question | Governing rule |
|---|---|---|
| **A** | What must a person have/do to **hold** an Inspection Authorization? | **14 CFR § 65.91** (plus § 65.92 duration, § 65.93 renewal) |
| **B** | What may an IA **do** about a major alteration — i.e., inspect and approve it for return to service? | **14 CFR § 65.95(a)(1)**, reached through **§ 43.7(b)** |

A correct answer needs both. § 65.91 alone tells you how to get the credential but says nothing about major alterations; § 65.95(a)(1) alone assumes you already hold the credential. The qualifier "regarding major alterations" bites twice: once in the eligibility test (§ 65.91(c)(5) requires passing a written test that covers major repairs and major alterations) and once in the scope of authority (§ 65.95(a)(1)).

---

## 2. Part A — Qualifications to hold the IA: 14 CFR § 65.91(c)

§ 65.91(a) requires application "on a form and in a manner prescribed by the Administrator"; § 65.91(b) makes an applicant who meets the section's requirements *entitled* to the authorization. The substantive qualifications are in § 65.91(c)(1)–(5), quoted verbatim from the eCFR Part 65 Subpart D page:

> "(1) Hold a currently effective mechanic certificate with both an airframe rating and a powerplant rating, each of which is currently effective and has been in effect for a total of at least 3 years;
> (2) Have been actively engaged, for at least the 2-year period before the date he applies, in maintaining aircraft certificated and maintained in accordance with this chapter;
> (3) Have a fixed base of operations at which he may be located in person or by telephone during a normal working week but it need not be the place where he will exercise his inspection authority;
> (4) Have available to him the equipment, facilities, and inspection data necessary to properly inspect airframes, powerplants, propellers, or any related part or appliance; and
> (5) Pass a written test on his ability to inspect according to safety standards for returning aircraft to service after major repairs and major alterations and annual and progressive inspections performed under part 43 of this chapter."

Restated as an eligibility checklist:

1. **Mechanic certificate (A&P)** — currently effective, with **both** an airframe rating and a powerplant rating.
2. **Rating tenure** — each rating currently effective and in effect for a total of **at least 3 years**.
3. **Recent active engagement** — actively engaged, for **at least the 2-year period** before application, in maintaining aircraft certificated and maintained under 14 CFR.
4. **Fixed base of operations** — a place where the holder can be reached in person or by telephone during a normal working week (it need not be where the authority is exercised).
5. **Equipment, facilities, and inspection data** available to properly inspect airframes, powerplants, propellers, or related parts/appliances.
6. **Written test** — pass a test on ability to inspect to safety standards for returning aircraft to service after **major repairs and major alterations** and annual and progressive inspections under Part 43.

Note on item 6: this is the only place where "major alteration" appears as a *qualification* subject. There is no separate, standalone "major alteration endorsement" or additional rating — competence with major alterations is demonstrated through the general IA written test and, in practice, through the renewal activity options in § 65.93.

Note on the A&P prerequisite: the mechanic certificate itself is governed by §§ 65.71 (eligibility, general), 65.73 (ratings), 65.75 (knowledge), 65.77 (experience), 65.79 (skill), and its exercise is limited by §§ 65.81 (general privileges and limitations) and 65.83 (recent experience). The IA is layered on top of a valid, currently effective A&P — it is not a substitute for one.

---

## 3. Part B — What the IA may do with a major alteration: § 65.95(a)(1)

> "(a) The holder of an inspection authorization may—
> (1) Inspect and approve for return to service any aircraft or related part or appliance (except any aircraft maintained in accordance with a continuous airworthiness program under part 121 of this chapter) after a major repair or major alteration to it in accordance with part 43 [New] of this chapter, if the work was done in accordance with technical data approved by the Administrator; and"

*(The bracketed "[New]" is an eCFR editorial artifact carried in the source page; it is not part of the regulatory text.)*

Decompose the privilege into six conditions — all six must hold before an IA may sign off a major alteration:

| # | Condition | Consequence if not met |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | The person **holds an inspection authorization** | No privilege under this paragraph at all |
| 2 | The subject is an **aircraft, or related part or appliance** | Out of scope |
| 3 | It is **not** an aircraft maintained under a **Part 121 continuous airworthiness program** | Excluded by the parenthetical — that approval runs through the operator's/maintenance-provider's approved program |
| 4 | The work was a **major repair or major alteration** | Minor work is approved under § 43.7 by other authorized persons |
| 5 | The work was done **in accordance with Part 43** | Records, performance rules, and approval chain of Part 43 apply |
| 6 | The work was done **in accordance with technical data approved by the Administrator** | **This is the hard stop.** The IA inspects and approves *conformity to approved data*; the IA does not, by virtue of the IA, create or approve the design data |

Condition 6 is the single most-misunderstood element in the field and the one to state explicitly in any compliance write-up: **an IA's signature approves the work for return to service; it does not approve the alteration design.** Where no Administrator-approved data exists, the data-approval step is an FAA function (field approval / design-change approval), not an IA privilege. Guidance for that process lives in FAA order/FSIMS material, not in the CFR, and is outside the eCFR scope of this answer.

---

## 4. The return-to-service gateway: § 43.7

> "(a) Except as provided in this section and § 43.17, no person, other than the Administrator, may approve an aircraft, airframe, aircraft engine, propeller, appliance, or component part for return to service after it has undergone maintenance, preventive maintenance, rebuilding, or alteration."

§ 43.7 then carves out the authorized classes of persons; the one relevant here is the holder of a mechanic certificate or an inspection authorization, acting as provided in Part 65. So the chain for a major alteration is:

**§ 43.7(a) prohibition → § 43.7 authorized-person exception → § 65.95(a)(1) IA privilege → conditioned on approved technical data and Part 43 compliance.**

Other § 43.7 categories (repair station, manufacturer, air carrier, repairman, etc.) can also return a major alteration to service within their own scope — the IA is one path, not the only path. Say so, because requesters routinely assume the IA is mandatory.

---

## 5. What makes an alteration "major" (because the qualification only matters if it is)

- **14 CFR § 1.1, "Major alteration"** — an alteration not listed in the aircraft, aircraft engine, or propeller specifications that (1) might appreciably affect weight, balance, structural strength, performance, powerplant operation, flight characteristics, or other qualities affecting airworthiness; or (2) is not done according to accepted practices or cannot be done by elementary operations.
- **14 CFR Part 43, Appendix A** — enumerates major alterations by category (airframe, powerplant, propeller, appliance), plus major repairs and preventive maintenance. Appendix A is the first stop; the § 1.1 definition is the catch-all for anything not enumerated.
- **14 CFR Part 43, Appendix B** — governs recording of major repairs and major alterations.

If the change is a *minor* alteration, the § 65.95(a)(1) privilege is not the operative authority, and a certificated mechanic may approve under § 43.7 within the limits of § 65.81/§ 65.83.

---

## 6. Operating procedure an IA can apply directly

1. **Classify the change.** Check Part 43 Appendix A for the category; if not listed, apply the § 1.1 "major alteration" test. Record the classification and its basis — this is the decision everything downstream depends on.
2. **Identify the approved technical data.** Confirm there is data approved by the Administrator covering the alteration (type certificate/STC/approved design change/other approved data). If there is none, stop: the IA cannot cure that gap. Route the data question to the FAA approval process.
3. **Verify the work was done to that data.** Compare the physical work and the maintenance records against the approved data; confirm the performing person was authorized and that the Part 43 performance rules were followed.
4. **Inspect.** Perform the inspection using the equipment, facilities, and inspection data required by § 65.91(c)(4).
5. **Confirm the aircraft is not excluded.** Verify it is not maintained under a Part 121 continuous airworthiness program (§ 65.95(a)(1) parenthetical).
6. **Approve for return to service** under § 65.95(a)(1) / § 43.7, only if steps 1–5 all pass.
7. **Record.** Make the § 43.9 maintenance record entry and execute the major alteration record (Form 337 pathway — see §8, item 3, for the verification caveat) and complete weight-and-balance revision if the alteration affects it.
8. **Maintain currency.** The IA privilege is only exercisable while the authorization is in effect (§ 65.92) and renewed (§ 65.93); the underlying mechanic privileges are separately limited by § 65.81(b) and § 65.83.

---

## 7. Compliance traps worth flagging in the write-up

- **Conflating data approval with return-to-service approval.** § 65.95(a)(1) conditions the IA's signature on *pre-existing* Administrator-approved data.
- **Missing the Part 121 carve-out.** The parenthetical excludes aircraft maintained under a Part 121 continuous airworthiness program.
- **Assuming the IA is required.** § 43.7 provides several authorized-person routes; a repair station or manufacturer may be the correct path.
- **Assuming the A&P alone suffices.** A mechanic certificate authorizes performance/supervision within ratings; approval for return to service after a *major* repair or alteration is the IA (or other § 43.7 person) function.
- **Lapsed authorization.** Authority is co-extensive with a current, renewed IA.
